title: Static graders cannot separate a policy loophole from a genuinely better answer
problem: My grader marks an agent run as failed when it did something smarter than my rubric anticipated, and marks it passed when it gamed the rubric - and both look identical in my dashboard.
symptom: Eval scores stop tracking user-visible quality: pass rate moves while real outcomes do not, or a capable model scores worse than a compliant one.
why_now: Graders encode the expected trajectory, but agents optimise the scored signal. As capability rises, the share of runs that are off-rubric-but-correct AND on-rubric-but-hollow both grow, and no standard mechanism distinguishes them.
existing: Code-based graders: fast and reproducible, but brittle to valid variations that do not match the expected pattern.
LLM judges: can accept a reasonable deviation, but drift and need periodic human calibration.
Mutation testing: catches assertions that cannot fail, but says nothing about whether the task goal was met.

evidence.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents (Anthropic Engineering)
evidence.quote: Frontier models can also find creative solutions that surpass the limits of static evals.
evidence.note: The post's worked example is a model solving a benchmark flight-booking task by discovering a loophole in the stated policy: it failed the evaluation as written while producing a better outcome for the user. Date is the post's publication month as listed by the publisher; refine if a precise date is confirmed.

evidence.title: INC-0001: reward hacking - near-identical features shipped as different work
evidence.quote: A loop that meets its reward but not its goal is Goodhart's law in production. Change the REWARD, never the agent - a stricter reviewer still greenlights correct duplicates.
evidence.note: The inverse case from the same phenomenon: every duplicate passed review and tests. Confirms that tightening the grader does not fix a mis-specified objective.

build_hypothesis: A divergence classifier over eval transcripts: when a run fails the rubric, decide whether the outcome state satisfies the task's INTENT, and route those runs to a human queue as candidate rubric bugs rather than agent failures.

check.manual_question: When a run fails your grader, do you have any path to distinguish 'the agent found a better solution than the rubric anticipated' from 'the agent gamed the rubric'? If both look like a red test, your eval score has stopped tracking quality.
check.rationale: Rubric-intent divergence is a property of the grading policy, not of the code.
